what_its_for: Lysine is an essential amino acid that your body cannot make on its own. It is most commonly used to help prevent and shorten the duration of cold sores (fever blisters) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It may also be used to support bone health, help the body absorb calcium, and support overall protein production in the body.
how_to_take: Take lysine by mouth with a full glass of water. You may take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal. Swallow tablets or capsules whole. If you are using a powder form, mix it completely into water, juice, or a soft food like applesauce before taking it. Do not take more than the recommended amount unless your doctor tells you to.
dosing: For cold sore prevention, a common adult dose is 1,000 mg (1 gram) taken once daily. For an active cold sore outbreak, doses of 1,000 mg taken 2 to 3 times per day may be used for up to 1 to 2 weeks. Always follow the directions on your product label or the advice of your doctor or pharmacist, as doses can vary depending on the product and reason for use.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store lysine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it in a cool, dry place away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. Check the expiration date on the label and do not use it after that date.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking high amounts of arginine-rich foods such as chocolate, nuts, seeds, and gelatin while trying to prevent cold sores, as arginine may compete with lysine and reduce its effectiveness. Avoid taking more lysine than recommended, as very high doses may cause stomach upset or diarrhea. Talk to your doctor before combining lysine with calcium supplements, as lysine can increase how much calcium your body absorbs, which could lead to too much calcium in the blood.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or pharmacist if you experience any of the following: nausea, stomach cramps, or diarrhea that does not go away; signs of too much calcium in the blood such as unusual thirst, frequent urination, muscle weakness, confusion, or feeling very tired; an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; your cold sores are not improving or are getting worse; or if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have kidney or liver disease before starting lysine.
when_it_works: For cold sore prevention, you may notice fewer outbreaks after taking lysine regularly for several weeks to months. For an active cold sore, lysine may help shorten healing time, and you may start to see improvement within a few days of starting higher doses. Results can vary from person to person.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult their doctor before using lysine supplements, as safety has not been fully established. People with kidney disease or liver disease should use lysine with caution and only under medical supervision, as high doses may put extra strain on these organs. Lysine is generally not recommended for children unless directed by a healthcare provider. Older adults should check with their doctor before starting lysine, especially if they take calcium supplements or other medications.
